content: Emtricitabine is a synthetic nucleoside analog of cytidine. Once inside the cell, it undergoes phosphorylation by cellular enzymes to form emtricitabine 5'-triphosphate. This active metabolite inhibits the activity of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate, deoxycytidine 5'-triphosphate. Additionally, it is incorporated into the growing viral DNA chain, leading to chain termination and halting viral replication. Emtricitabine 5'-triphosphate exhibits weak inhibitory effects on mammalian DNA polymerases α, β, ε, and mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ. The antiviral activity of emtricitabine has been evaluated in cell culture against both laboratory and clinical isolates of HIV-1. These studies were conducted in lymphoblastoid cell lines, the MAGI-CCR5 cell line, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. In combination drug trials, emtricitabine demonstrated additive to synergistic effects when used with other nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as abacavir, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, zalcitabine, and zidovudine; non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as delavirdine, efavirenz, and nevirapine; and protease inhibitors such as amprenavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, and saquinavir. The in vivo activity of emtricitabine was assessed in two clinical trials involving 101 subjects who received 25–400 mg of emtricitabine (EMTRIVA) daily as monotherapy for 10–14 days. A significant reduction in HIV-1 RNA levels, by approximately 0.9 log10, was observed at a dose of 200 mg administered once or twice daily. Emtricitabine-resistant isolates of HIV-1 have been identified both in cell culture and in vivo. Genotypic analysis of these isolates revealed that reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine was associated with a substitution in the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase gene at codon 184, resulting in the replacement of methionine with valine or isoleucine (M184V/I). Such resistant isolates have been recovered from some patients treated with emtricitabine alone or in combination with other antiretroviral agents. Among subjects with virologic failure, approximately 5% exhibited reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine, with resistance linked to the M184V/I substitutions in the reverse transcriptase gene. In a clinical trial involving treatment-naive subjects, resistance analysis was performed on HIV-1 isolates from individuals experiencing virologic failure with greater than 400 copies/mL of HIV-1 RNA at Week 144 or upon early discontinuation. The development of efavirenz resistance-associated substitutions occurred most frequently and was similar across treatment arms. The M184V amino acid substitution, associated with resistance to emtricitabine and lamivudine, was observed in 2 out of 19 analyzed isolates in the emtricitabine + tenofovir group and in 10 out of 29 analyzed isolates in the lamivudine/zidovudine group. Through 144 weeks of Study 934, no subjects developed a detectable K65R substitution in their HIV-1 as determined by standard genotypic analysis. Cross-resistance among certain nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) has been documented. Emtricitabine-resistant isolates (M184V/I) were cross-resistant to lamivudine and zalcitabine but retained sensitivity to didanosine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine, and NNRTIs (delavirdine, efavirenz, and nevirapine). HIV-1 isolates containing the K65R substitution, selected in vivo by abacavir, didanosine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine, demonstrated reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine. However, viruses harboring substitutions conferring resistance to stavudine and zidovudine (M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y/F, K219Q/E) or didanosine (L74V) remained sensitive to emtricitabine. Additionally, HIV-1 containing the K103N substitution, associated with resistance to NNRTIs, was susceptible to emtricitabine.
